newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - JAN 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - JAN 7.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The state is spreading its net wide to catch all possible loopholes in avoiding the new tax on real estate. A special form dubbed E9 will require details on location, size and value of real estate and will be processed by the finance ministry along with tax declarations in March. Substantial fines will be imposed on those who do not submit the form or give inaccurate or misleading information.

--Meanwhile, loopholes have been found in the government's new legislation on taxation of state titles. The finance ministry is working with the Bank of Greece to close them. Central bank officials say that all inter-state agreements on double taxation will need to be examined to best deal with the problem.

--The Bank of Greece's desire to ensure the stability of the drachma and maintain the anti-inflationary character of exchange policy leaves it cautiously reserved about the speedy de-escalation of interest rates that the state and commercial banks are pursuing. Interbank rates are expected to remain at high levels.
--Many bankers believe that interest rates have reached excessively low rates, in contrast to the national economy and finance ministries which believes there are still margins for reduction.

--Alpha Credit Bank expects to see a signficant improvement in its 1996 performance and the administration has already said it will increase its share capital by 60 billion drachmas. Net profits are expected to reach the 62 billion drachma mark, an increase of 20 percent over 1995 figures.

--Prime Minister Costas Simitis and Development Minister Vasso Papandreou's meetings next week with the Russian energy minister and the president of Gazprom, the company in charge of the natural gas pipeline to Greece, will mark a new era in the country's energy sector.

--Although telecoms organisation OTE has adjusted prices, other state utilities are not expected to increase tariffs before July. Increases for cigarettes and alcohol as well as car insurance premiums will also mark smaller increases than last year, in an effort to keep a tight rein on inflation.
--A two billion drachma loan from the National Bank has averted disaster for Softex, the state-run paper manufacturers.

--The increase in share prices for the Alpha Credit Bank by 7.0 percent over the last two days has bolstered reports of the participation of an international strategic investor in the bank's share capital. Reports name the investor as Manufacturers Hanover but others have denied this and say there is an institutional investor who will participate in the increase in share capital. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
